UNIT 9: THE ROCK CYCLE

KEY THEME
- Rocks are constantly formed, changed, broken down and reformed through the rock cycle.
- Learning outcomes: identify and describe the endogenic and exogenic processes in the rock cycle; identify the three main categories of rock; describe how igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks form, with Irish examples.

KEY TERMS
- Rock cycle: the continuous process that forms, changes, destroys and recycles rocks on Earth. It has no start or end.
- Igneous rock: forms when magma or lava cools and solidifies.
- Sedimentary rock: made from layers of compacted and cemented sediments (broken rock, plant or animal material); often has fossils.
- Metamorphic rock: forms when any existing rock is changed by heat and/or pressure without melting.
- Endogenic processes: internal forces driven by heat from the Earth's core and the movement of tectonic plates (plate movement, volcanism, burial, heat, pressure, melting).
- Exogenic processes: external forces on the Earth's surface - weathering, erosion and deposition.
- Magma crystallisation: magma cooling and solidifying into igneous rock, forming crystals.
- Magma cooling: the process by which liquid magma cools and becomes solid, forming crystals of different minerals.
- Weathering: breaking down rocks into smaller pieces.
- Erosion: transportation of rock particles by natural forces (water, wind, ice).
- Sediment: small pieces of rock or minerals; the raw material for sedimentary rocks.
- Compaction: pressing sediments together by weight.
- Cementation: minerals sticking sediments together.
- Lithification: turning loose sediments into solid rock by compacting and cementing the particles together.
- Strata: layers of sediment or rock. Stratified = layered.
- Bedding planes: horizontal gaps separating the layers of sedimentary rock.
- Joints: vertical cracks in rock (in limestone, formed by plate movement folding and breaking the rock).
- Permeable: lets water pass easily through the rock.
- Organic: from plants and animals. Inorganic: from minerals.
- Intrusive igneous rock: magma cools and hardens beneath the surface (e.g. granite).
- Extrusive igneous rock: lava cools and hardens on the surface (e.g. basalt).
- Metamorphism: the endogenic process where heat and/or pressure changes a rock's structure, minerals and texture, without melting it.
- Foliation: when a metamorphic rock has distinct repeated layers; pressure forces minerals to line up in flat parallel layers, giving a banded or striped look (e.g. schist, gneiss). Non-foliated rocks (e.g. marble, quartzite) are crystalline without bands.
- Magma intrusion: hot magma forcing its way into surrounding cooler rock.
- Aureole: the zone around an intrusion where the parent rock is changed into metamorphic rock.

THE ROCK CYCLE (Figures 9.1 and 9.3 in words)
- Magma cools (crystallises) to form igneous rock.
- Surface rocks are broken down by weathering and erosion into sediment.
- Sediment is transported and deposited, usually under water.
- Compaction and cementation (lithification) turn sediment into sedimentary rock.
- Rocks buried deep underground meet heat and pressure and become metamorphic rock.
- Further burial or heat melts rock back into magma, restarting the cycle.
- Any rock can become any other: igneous can become sedimentary, metamorphic or new igneous; sedimentary can become metamorphic, igneous or new sedimentary; metamorphic can become igneous, sedimentary or new metamorphic.
- Changes usually take millions of years, though events like eruptions can speed up parts of the cycle.
- Endogenic forces like tectonic activity uplift and expose rocks; exogenic weathering and erosion then break them down. Agents such as rivers, wind, glaciers and waves carry sediment, usually to the seafloor.
- Slow cooling underground gives large crystals (granite); rapid cooling at the surface gives fine crystals (basalt).

WEATHERING (an exogenic process)
- Weathering is the breakdown and decay of rocks into smaller pieces (sediment) at the Earth's surface.
- Mechanical (physical) weathering: physically breaks rock apart without changing its mineral make-up. Examples: freeze-thaw and exfoliation.
- Chemical weathering: changes the mineral composition of rock. Examples: carbonation and oxidation.

Freeze-thaw action (example: Croagh Patrick, Co. Mayo)
- Happens in upland areas where temperatures go above and below freezing.
- By day rainwater enters cracks in the rock (e.g. daytime 10 degrees C).
- At night temperatures drop below 0 degrees C (e.g. -3 degrees C) and the water freezes.
- Ice expands by about 9% in volume, putting pressure on the rock and widening the cracks.
- Repeated, this makes pieces break off, forming loose material called scree on steep slopes.

Exfoliation (example: Sahara Desert)
- Happens in hot deserts with a large diurnal range (big difference between day and night temperatures).
- By day high temperatures (40 degrees C) heat the outer layer, which expands.
- At night temperatures drop (-10 degrees C) and the outer layer cools and contracts.
- Daily repetition stresses the outer layer; cracks form, join up and the outer layer peels away. Also called 'onion peeling'.

Carbonation (example: The Burren, Co. Clare)
- Rainwater mixes with carbon dioxide in the air to form weak carbonic acid.
- This dissolves calcium carbonate in limestone, forming soluble calcium bicarbonate, which is carried away in solution.
- Limestone is permeable, so the acid flows through and attacks cracks and joints, widening them and weakening the rock.

Oxidation (example: MacGillycuddy's Reeks, Co. Kerry)
- Oxygen (usually with water) reacts with minerals like iron in rock, forming reddish, rusty iron oxide.
- Iron oxide is soft, so the rock weakens, crumbles and breaks down. Happens in sandstone landscapes.

FORMATION OF IGNEOUS ROCKS
- Igneous rocks form when molten rock from deep in the Earth cools and solidifies, either below the surface or after erupting from a volcano.
- Magma forms deep in the crust or upper mantle at high temperatures (often 600-1,300 degrees C), sometimes with reduced pressure, causing partial melting of rocks.
- Magma is less dense than surrounding rock, so it rises - sometimes erupting, sometimes cooling at depth.

Granite - intrusive igneous rock
- Forms at convergent plate boundaries (subduction zones).
- Irish examples: the Leinster Batholith (Dublin-Wicklow Mountains) and granite outcrops of Donegal.
- About 400 million years ago the Eurasian and North American plates collided (Caledonian Orogeny). Magma formed deep underground.
- It cooled very slowly, so large crystals grew (crystallisation), forming coarse-grained granite made of quartz, feldspar and mica.
- Over millions of years weathering and erosion wore away the rock above, exposing granite in the Dublin-Wicklow Mountains.
- Endogenic conditions needed: deep burial, high temperatures and slow cooling.
- Appearance: light in colour, often grey or pink, coarse-grained with visible crystals (looks like a firelighter).
- Geofact: the Leinster Batholith lies under the Dublin-Wicklow and Blackstairs Mountains; one of the largest batholiths in western Europe, covering 1,500 square km.

Basalt - extrusive igneous rock
- Forms at divergent plate boundaries. Found at the Giant's Causeway and the Antrim-Derry Plateau.
- About 60 million years ago, basic lava flowed out of cracks (fissure eruptions) where the Eurasian and American plates were separating.
- The lava cooled quickly, contracted and cracked into hexagonal columns: about 40,000 interlocking, mostly hexagonal columns - the 'stepping stones' of the Giant's Causeway.
- Contact with air or water cools lava quickly, so large crystals cannot form: basalt is fine-grained with a glassy texture.
- Appearance: dark (black or dark grey), small or no visible crystals.
- Endogenic processes drive magma generation and its rise.

FORMATION OF SEDIMENTARY ROCKS
- Formed from sediments of older rocks and organic remains, usually on lake and ocean beds, in layers (strata) separated by bedding planes.
- Stages:
  1. Weathering and erosion: rocks broken into sediment by physical and chemical weathering (also biological). Particles may be organic or inorganic.
  2. Transportation: sediment moved by water, wind, ice or gravity.
  3. Deposition: sediment settles in layers (strata), commonly on sea and lake beds but also on land.
  4. Burial and compaction: new layers bury older ones; the weight squeezes deeper layers, reducing pore space and squeezing out water.
  5. Cementation and lithification: minerals in groundwater (silica or calcite) seep between grains and glue them together; loose sediment becomes solid rock.

LIMESTONE
- Origin: mainly the remains of marine organisms and plants. Example: the Burren, Co. Clare; also the Central Lowlands.
- Most Irish limestone formed about 350 million years ago when Ireland lay under a warm, shallow tropical sea.
- Bones and shells of sea life (rich in calcium carbonate, CaCO3) settled on the sea floor and mixed with fine mud, building layers.
- Deposition was not continuous; interruptions created bedding planes.
- Compaction squeezed out water and reduced pores; dissolved calcite carried by groundwater cemented the grains (cementation). Together = lithification, forming thick limestone beds over millions of years.
- Features: bedding planes and vertical joints (from later Earth movements) give a blocky structure; permeable (water flows down joints and bedding planes); fossils are common (evidence of marine origin, e.g. the Burren).
- Appearance: grey, layered, sometimes with fossils; easily weathered by rainwater.
- Chalk: a soft, white, pure form of limestone, made almost entirely of the microscopic skeletons of plankton that lived over 90 million years ago.

SANDSTONE
- Origin: accumulation and lithification of sand-sized grains, mainly quartz or feldspar. Example: MacGillycuddy's Reeks, Co. Kerry (Old Red Sandstone); also the Comeragh Mountains.
- Weathering breaks older rocks into sand grains.
- Rivers, wind or glaciers transport the grains, sorting them by size: heavier, coarser grains settle first; finer grains travel further.
- When the transporting agent loses energy, grains settle in horizontal layers - in river deltas, beaches, deserts and lake beds.
- Layers build up and compact the grains. Minerals such as calcite, silica or iron oxide from groundwater build up round the grains and cement them. Compaction + cementation = lithification into sandstone.
- Features: colour varies with minerals - iron oxide gives red/rusty colour (white grains are quartz); usually red, brown or yellow; rough texture; visible layers and bedding planes; porous and permeable.
- Geofact: Carrauntoohil in the MacGillycuddy's Reeks is Ireland's highest mountain at 1,038 m.

OTHER SEDIMENTARY ROCKS
- Shale: formed from clay and silt.
- Coal: formed from compressed plant material.
- Gypsum: formed from evaporating saline (salt) waters.

FORMATION OF METAMORPHIC ROCKS
- Existing rocks (igneous, sedimentary or older metamorphic) are subjected to great heat, pressure or both. The rock does not melt, but its structure, minerals and texture change (metamorphism - an endogenic process).
Main processes:
1. Heat: high temperatures from nearby magma or deep burial make minerals recrystallise (change shape, size or structure) or form new minerals. This is thermal or contact metamorphism, when hot magma forces into cooler rock (magma intrusion).
2. Pressure: deep burial or mountain building squeezes and sometimes folds rocks, aligning minerals into parallel bands. This is dynamic metamorphism, often along fault lines or transform boundaries.
3. Combined heat and pressure: bigger changes over large areas, often where plates collide - regional metamorphism.
4. Recrystallisation: minerals in the parent rock are rearranged or replaced by new minerals stable in the new conditions, without melting.
Types of metamorphism:
- Regional: heat and pressure over wide areas, usually at convergent boundaries. Example: marble.
- Contact/thermal: mainly heat from magma or lava touching surrounding rock. Example: quartzite. Around a batholith, the changed zone is the aureole.
- Dynamic: intense pressure and movement along faults where rocks grind past each other. Example: mylonite.
Parent rocks (Figure 9.44): limestone becomes marble; sandstone becomes quartzite; shale becomes slate (then schist); granite becomes gneiss. Gneiss is foliated; quartzite is non-foliated.

MARBLE
- A hard, coarse, crystalline, non-foliated rock formed from limestone; known for durability.
- Shells and bones rich in calcium carbonate formed limestone on the seabed.
- Regional metamorphism: in Ireland, tectonic activity during the Caledonian orogeny about 450 million years ago forced the limestone deep underground. Temperatures of 500-800 degrees C and great pressure over millions of years caused metamorphism.
- Calcite recrystallises, removing fossils and original sedimentary features, forming a denser rock. More heat and pressure = larger calcite crystals.
- Colour comes from impurities: Kilkenny marble is black (carbon); Connemara marble (Co. Galway) is green (serpentine); Cork marble is red (iron oxides). Ranges from white to green, red or black; hard, smooth, with a decorative shine.

QUARTZITE
- A hard, coarse, non-foliated rock formed from sandstone; durable, grainy, often sparkling with quartz crystals.
- Sand grains (mainly quartz) deposited by rivers, wind or sea were compacted and cemented into sandstone.
- Contact (thermal) metamorphism: folding during the Caledonian orogeny about 400 million years ago, when the Eurasian and North American plates collided, let magma squeeze between folded layers, superheating the sandstone.
- The heat made the quartz grains cement together and recrystallise into a much harder, denser rock.
- Pure quartzite is white or grey; iron oxide can make it pink or red. Very hard, glassy, very resistant to erosion.
- Examples: Great and Little Sugar Loaf, Co. Wicklow (from sandstone deposited over 500 million years ago, changed in the Caledonian orogeny); Croagh Patrick, Co. Mayo (steep, rugged quartzite slopes that resist erosion).

EXAM SKILLS
- SEC Ordinary Level: Irish examples - volcanic landform: lava plateau (Antrim); sedimentary rock: limestone; metamorphic rock: quartzite; fold mountain range: Wicklow Mountains.
- SEC Higher Level: a rock type formed by lithification - limestone (the Burren), shown on a map of Ireland.

rows.prompt: What are endogenic processes?
options: Internal forces driven by Earth's heat and plate movement
External forces like wind and rain
The settling of sediment in layers
The weathering of rock at the surface
rows.explanation: Endogenic processes are internal forces such as heat, pressure, melting and plate movement.

rows.prompt: Which of these is an exogenic process?
rows.explanation: Exogenic processes act on the surface: weathering, erosion and deposition.

rows.prompt: What happens if a metamorphic rock is heated so much that it melts?
rows.explanation: Melting turns any rock back into magma, restarting the rock cycle.

rows.prompt: What is lithification?
options: Turning loose sediment into solid rock
rows.explanation: Lithification is compaction and cementation turning loose sediment into solid rock.

rows.prompt: What is the difference between mechanical and chemical weathering?
options: Mechanical breaks rock without changing its minerals
Mechanical changes the minerals in rock
rows.explanation: Mechanical weathering breaks rock physically; chemical weathering changes its mineral composition.

rows.prompt: By about how much does water expand when it freezes?
rows.explanation: Water expands by about 9% as it turns to ice, widening cracks in rock.

rows.prompt: What loose material does freeze-thaw produce on mountain slopes?
rows.explanation: Pieces broken off by freeze-thaw collect as scree, e.g. on Croagh Patrick.

rows.prompt: Exfoliation happens mainly where there is:
rows.explanation: Hot deserts like the Sahara have big day-night temperature differences that make rock layers peel.

rows.prompt: Which acid dissolves limestone during carbonation?
rows.explanation: Rainwater and carbon dioxide form weak carbonic acid, which dissolves calcium carbonate.

rows.prompt: Oxidation of iron in rock produces what?
rows.explanation: Iron reacts with oxygen to form soft, rusty iron oxide that weakens rock.

rows.prompt: Which Irish location is the example of oxidation in sandstone?
rows.explanation: Oxidation occurs in sandstone landscapes such as MacGillycuddy's Reeks, Co. Kerry.

rows.prompt: What type of rock forms when magma cools slowly beneath the surface?
rows.explanation: Slow cooling underground lets large crystals grow, forming granite.

rows.prompt: Granite is made mainly of which three minerals?
rows.explanation: Granite is coarse-grained rock of quartz, feldspar and mica crystals.

rows.prompt: Why does basalt have very small crystals?
rows.explanation: Lava cooling quickly in air or water stops large crystals forming, so basalt is fine-grained.

rows.prompt: At what type of plate boundary did the basalt of the Giant's Causeway form?
rows.explanation: Basic lava flowed out of fissures where the Eurasian and American plates were separating.

rows.prompt: About how many columns make up the Giant's Causeway?
rows.explanation: Cooling lava contracted into about 40,000 interlocking, mostly hexagonal columns.

rows.prompt: Magma usually forms at what range of temperatures?
rows.explanation: Magma forms deep in the crust or upper mantle, often at 600-1,300 degrees C.

rows.prompt: What are bedding planes?
options: Bands of minerals in metamorphic rock
rows.explanation: Bedding planes are the horizontal gaps separating layers (strata) of sedimentary rock.

rows.prompt: During compaction, what happens to the sediment?
options: Weight squeezes out water and reduces pores
rows.explanation: The weight of overlying layers presses grains together, squeezing out water.

rows.prompt: Which minerals in groundwater act as cement in sedimentary rock?
rows.explanation: Silica or calcite seep between grains and glue them together.

rows.prompt: About how long ago did most Irish limestone form?
rows.explanation: Most Irish limestone formed about 350 million years ago in a warm, shallow tropical sea.

rows.prompt: Why is limestone permeable?
options: Water passes through its joints and bedding planes
It is made of sand grains
rows.explanation: Vertical joints and bedding planes let water flow down through limestone.

rows.prompt: What do fossils in the Burren's limestone tell us?
rows.explanation: Fossils of marine life are evidence that the limestone formed on the sea floor.

rows.prompt: Chalk is made mainly from what?
rows.explanation: Chalk is a pure limestone made of microscopic plankton skeletons from over 90 million years ago.

rows.prompt: What gives sandstone a red or rusty colour?
rows.explanation: Iron oxide coating and cement gives sandstone its red colour.

rows.prompt: Coal is formed from:
rows.explanation: Coal forms from compressed plant material.

rows.prompt: Which statement about metamorphic rocks is true?
options: They form only from sedimentary rocks
They form when rock melts completely
They form when heat or pressure changes rock without melting it
rows.explanation: Metamorphism changes any existing rock by heat and/or pressure, without melting.

rows.prompt: Which type of metamorphism is caused mainly by heat from a magma intrusion?
rows.explanation: Contact or thermal metamorphism occurs where hot magma touches cooler rock.

rows.prompt: Regional metamorphism usually happens:
options: Over wide areas where plates collide
rows.explanation: Regional metamorphism involves heat and pressure over large areas, usually at convergent boundaries.

rows.prompt: Connemara marble is green because of which mineral?
rows.explanation: Serpentine makes Connemara marble green; carbon makes Kilkenny marble black.

rows.prompt: Quartzite forms from which parent rock?
rows.explanation: Heat recrystallises the quartz grains in sandstone into quartzite.

rows.prompt: Which rock is foliated?
rows.explanation: Gneiss has bands of aligned minerals (foliation); marble and quartzite are non-foliated.

rows.prompt: Describe the rock cycle in your own words, naming the three rock types.
rows.model_answer: The rock cycle is the continuous process that forms, changes, destroys and recycles rocks. Magma cools to form igneous rock; weathering and erosion break rocks into sediment, which is deposited and lithified into sedimentary rock. Heat and pressure change buried rock into metamorphic rock, and melting turns it back into magma.

rows.prompt: Explain how freeze-thaw weathering breaks down rock. Name an Irish example.
rows.model_answer: In upland areas rainwater enters cracks in rock by day. At night temperatures drop below 0 degrees C and the water freezes, expanding by about 9% and widening the cracks. Repeated freezing and thawing makes pieces break off and collect as scree, e.g. on Croagh Patrick, Co. Mayo.

rows.prompt: Explain how carbonation weathers limestone.
rows.model_answer: Rainwater mixes with carbon dioxide to form weak carbonic acid. This dissolves the calcium carbonate in limestone, forming soluble calcium bicarbonate that is carried away. Because limestone is permeable, the acid attacks joints and cracks, widening them, as in the Burren, Co. Clare.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between intrusive and extrusive igneous rocks, with an Irish example of each.
rows.model_answer: Intrusive rocks form when magma cools slowly underground, giving large crystals, e.g. granite in the Leinster Batholith (Wicklow Mountains). Extrusive rocks form when lava cools quickly on the surface, giving tiny crystals, e.g. basalt at the Giant's Causeway.

rows.prompt: List the stages in the formation of sedimentary rock.
rows.model_answer: Weathering and erosion break rocks into sediment. The sediment is transported by water, wind, ice or gravity and deposited in layers (strata). Burial and compaction squeeze the layers, and cementation by minerals like silica or calcite glues the grains, so lithification forms solid rock.

rows.prompt: Describe the features of limestone.
rows.model_answer: Limestone is grey and layered, with bedding planes and vertical joints that give it a blocky structure. It is permeable, so water flows down through joints and bedding planes. It often contains fossils, which show it formed in a warm, shallow sea, as in the Burren.

rows.prompt: Explain how marble forms from limestone.
rows.model_answer: During the Caledonian orogeny about 450 million years ago, limestone was forced deep underground. Temperatures of 500-800 degrees C and great pressure caused regional metamorphism. The calcite recrystallised, removing fossils and layers and forming hard, dense, crystalline marble, e.g. Connemara or Kilkenny marble.

rows.prompt: What is foliation?
rows.model_answer: Foliation is when a metamorphic rock has distinct repeated layers. Pressure inside the Earth forces minerals to line up in flat parallel layers, giving the rock a banded or striped look. Schist and gneiss are foliated rocks.

rows.prompt: Examine the formation of igneous rocks, with reference to Irish examples. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: Igneous rocks form when magma cools and solidifies, a process called magma crystallisation. Magma forms deep in the crust or upper mantle at temperatures of about 600-1,300 degrees C, when rocks partly melt. Being less dense than the rock around it, magma rises. Granite is an intrusive igneous rock. About 400 million years ago, during the Caledonian Orogeny, the Eurasian and North American plates collided at a convergent boundary and magma formed deep underground. It cooled very slowly, so large crystals of quartz, feldspar and mica grew, forming coarse-grained, light grey or pink granite. Over millions of years weathering and erosion removed the overlying rocks, exposing the granite of the Leinster Batholith in the Dublin-Wicklow Mountains, which covers about 1,500 square km. Granite is also found in Donegal. Basalt is an extrusive igneous rock. About 60 million years ago the Eurasian and American plates separated at a divergent boundary. Basic lava flowed out of fissures onto the surface in Antrim. In contact with air and water it cooled quickly, so only tiny crystals formed, giving dark, fine-grained basalt. As it cooled the lava contracted and cracked into about 40,000 hexagonal columns, forming the Giant's Causeway and the Antrim-Derry Plateau.
rows.marking_scheme: Named Irish examples 2m + 2m (e.g. Leinster Batholith/granite; Giant's Causeway/basalt). Examination: 13 SRPs x 2m = 26m, e.g. magma crystallisation; temperature 600-1,300 C; magma rises as less dense; intrusive vs extrusive; convergent/Caledonian 400 million; slow cooling, large crystals; quartz, feldspar, mica; erosion exposes granite; 1,500 sq km; divergent 60 million; fissure eruptions; rapid cooling, fine-grained; contraction into 40,000 hexagonal columns. Total 30 marks.

rows.prompt: Describe the main stages in the formation of sedimentary rock and apply them to one sedimentary rock you have studied. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Sedimentary rock forms in stages. First, weathering and erosion break older rocks into sediment. Second, the sediment is transported by water, wind, ice or gravity. Third, it is deposited in layers (strata), usually on sea or lake beds. Fourth, new layers bury the older ones and their weight compacts them, squeezing out water. Fifth, minerals like calcite or silica cement the grains together, and lithification forms solid rock. Limestone in the Burren, Co. Clare formed about 350 million years ago in a warm, shallow tropical sea. Shells and bones of sea creatures, rich in calcium carbonate, settled on the sea floor with fine mud. Breaks in deposition created bedding planes. Compaction squeezed out water and calcite cemented the remains, forming grey, layered, fossil-rich limestone.
rows.marking_scheme: Stages: 5 SRPs x 2m = 10m (weathering/erosion; transport; deposition in strata; compaction; cementation/lithification). Named rock and example 2m. Application: 4 SRPs x 2m = 8m (e.g. 350 million years; warm shallow sea; CaCO3 shells; bedding planes; calcite cement; fossils). Total 20 marks.

rows.prompt: Compare contact (thermal) metamorphism and regional metamorphism, giving one Irish example of each. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: Metamorphism is when existing rock is changed by heat and/or pressure without melting, an endogenic process. Minerals recrystallise or are replaced by new ones, changing the rock's structure and texture. Contact (thermal) metamorphism is caused mainly by heat. When hot magma intrudes into cooler surrounding rock, the heat bakes the nearby rock. The changed zone around the intrusion is called the aureole, so it affects a fairly small area. Example: quartzite at the Sugarloaf, Co. Wicklow. During the Caledonian orogeny about 400 million years ago, the Eurasian and North American plates collided and magma squeezed up between folded layers of sandstone, superheating it. The quartz grains recrystallised into very hard, white or grey, sparkling quartzite that resists erosion, also seen at Croagh Patrick. Regional metamorphism is caused by both heat and pressure over wide areas, usually where plates collide at convergent boundaries. Example: marble. In the Caledonian orogeny about 450 million years ago, limestone was forced deep underground, where temperatures of 500-800 degrees C and great pressure acted over millions of years. The calcite recrystallised, removing fossils and bedding, forming dense marble. More heat and pressure gives larger crystals. Impurities give colour: Connemara marble is green (serpentine) and Kilkenny marble is black (carbon). Both quartzite and marble are non-foliated.
rows.marking_scheme: Definition of metamorphism 2m. Named Irish examples 2m + 2m (e.g. Sugarloaf quartzite; Connemara/Kilkenny marble). Comparison: 12 SRPs x 2m = 24m, at least 4 SRPs on each type, e.g. heat from magma intrusion; aureole/local area; sandstone parent; Caledonian 400 million; recrystallised quartz; resistant/Croagh Patrick; heat AND pressure; wide areas/convergent boundaries; limestone parent; 450 million; 500-800 C; fossils removed; colour from impurities. Total 30 marks.

rows.prompt: Explain one process of mechanical weathering and one process of chemical weathering. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Mechanical weathering - exfoliation: in hot deserts like the Sahara there is a large diurnal range. By day temperatures of about 40 degrees C heat the outer layer of rock, which expands. At night temperatures fall to about -10 degrees C, so the outer layer cools and contracts. This daily heating and cooling stresses the outer layer, cracks form and join up, and the layer peels away like an onion. The rock breaks without its minerals changing. Chemical weathering - oxidation: oxygen, usually with water, reacts with iron in rocks such as sandstone. The iron changes into reddish, rusty iron oxide, which is soft. This weakens the rock so it crumbles and breaks into smaller pieces, as in the MacGillycuddy's Reeks, Co. Kerry.
rows.marking_scheme: Each process 10m: named process 2m + 4 SRPs x 2m (e.g. large diurnal range; 40 C expansion; -10 C contraction; cracks join, outer layer peels; no chemical change / oxygen + water; iron reacts; rusty iron oxide; soft, rock crumbles; named example). Total 20 marks.
